client: I've been feeling so overwhelmed lately trying to balance grad school and my job at the coffee shop. I want to do really well in my program, but I'm exhausted all the time and I'm worried I'm not performing well enough at either place. To be honest, I'm not sure talking about it will help - the workload isn't going to change, so what's the point?
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a heavy load right now, and it makes complete sense that you'd feel exhausted trying to meet all these demands. I hear your skepticism about talking helping, but sometimes just naming these pressures can create space to explore new ways of coping—what thoughts come up when you notice yourself feeling overwhelmed?

client: I guess when I feel overwhelmed, my brain just starts racing with thoughts like "I can't handle this" and "I'm going to fail at everything." It's like this wave of panic hits me, and then I just shut down. I don't know if talking about it helps because the feelings still feel so real and intense in the moment.
therapist: Those automatic thoughts sound incredibly intense and painful when they hit you—it's understandable they'd lead to shutting down. I wonder if we could explore together how those thoughts might be coloring your experience of the situation—what typically happens right before these waves of panic appear?

client:
It usually happens when I'm alone at night trying to fall asleep. My mind starts racing about all the things I didn't get done that day, and then I get this crushing feeling that I'm failing at everything. 

I don't know if exploring the thoughts will help though - they feel so real in the moment, like obvious truths about how terrible I am. It's not just coloring my experience, it IS my experience when it happens.
therapist: It makes sense that these thoughts feel absolutely true in those vulnerable nighttime moments—our minds can be convincing storytellers when we're tired and alone. I wonder if we could gently examine whether these nighttime thoughts might be speaking in absolutes ("everything," "terrible") that don't leave room for the more balanced truth? What might your daytime self say about these nighttime conclusions?

client: I get what you're saying about absolutes, but in those moments, it really does feel like everything is terrible. My daytime self might try to be more logical, but it’s hard to connect with that when I’m lying there in the dark, feeling completely alone. Even if I know it’s not entirely rational, it still feels so real and overwhelming.
therapist: It sounds like there's a real disconnect between your daytime awareness and those nighttime experiences—that must feel incredibly frustrating. I wonder if we could explore ways to help your daytime self leave little reminders or comforts for your nighttime self to find? What small gesture of kindness might feel meaningful to receive in those difficult moments?

client: I don't know... the idea of leaving myself notes or something feels kind of silly. When I'm in that anxious nighttime spiral, I don't think a sticky note on my nightstand would make any difference. It's like my brain completely takes over and logic goes out the window.
therapist: I hear how deeply consuming those nighttime spirals feel—like they override any logical intervention. That must make the idea of notes seem woefully inadequate against such powerful experiences. What if we thought of this less as a solution and more as an experiment—just to observe what happens when we try to interrupt the spiral with something tangible?

client: I get what you're saying about treating it like an experiment, but when I'm in that spiral at 3 AM, even reaching for a notebook feels impossible. My brain just keeps screaming that writing things down won't change anything. I've tried similar things before and ended up staring at blank pages feeling even more hopeless.
therapist: It sounds like you've had some painful experiences where attempts to intervene actually made the spiral feel worse—that's important information about what doesn't work for you. I wonder if we could explore what that "screaming" part is trying to protect you from in those moments?

client: I don't know... that screaming feeling is just so overwhelming when it happens. It's like my brain is trying to protect me from failing or looking stupid, but it goes way overboard. When you ask me to explore it, I get nervous that focusing on it will just make the anxiety worse.
therapist: It makes complete sense that you'd be wary of diving deeper into something that already feels so overwhelming—your caution about not wanting to amplify the anxiety is very wise. I wonder if we could approach this differently by exploring what small moments of relief might look like, even if they don't "solve" the spiral? What tiny thing sometimes helps even just a little when you're in that space?

client: I appreciate you saying that, but honestly even the idea of finding small moments of relief feels exhausting right now. When the anxiety gets bad, everything feels pointless—like I'm just going through the motions without any real hope of feeling better. Sometimes watching TV helps for a few minutes, but then I just feel guilty for wasting time.
therapist: It sounds like even the temporary escapes come with their own painful aftermath of guilt—that must make it so hard to find any true rest. I wonder if we could gently explore what makes those moments of watching TV feel like "wasting time" rather than the necessary self-care they might actually be?

client: I know logically that rest is important, but when I'm watching TV, this voice in my head keeps saying I should be doing something productive instead. It's like I can't fully relax because I feel guilty the whole time, which kind of defeats the purpose. Maybe it's because my parents always emphasized being busy as a virtue when I was growing up.
therapist: It sounds like this guilt around resting runs deep, shaped by those early messages about productivity being tied to worth—no wonder relaxation feels so fraught for you. What might it feel like to experiment with reframing TV time as "productive rest" that actually fuels your ability to meet your goals?

client:
I get what you're saying about reframing rest as productive, but it's hard to shake this nagging voice that tells me I'm just making excuses to be lazy. Even when I try to watch TV, I keep checking the time and thinking about all the things I *should* be doing instead. 

The idea that rest fuels productivity makes logical sense, but my gut still reacts like I'm doing something wrong whenever I'm not actively accomplishing things. It's like my brain has this automatic alarm system for "wasting time."
therapist: That automatic alarm system sounds exhausting to live with—like you can never truly switch off without it blaring at you. I wonder if we could explore what might happen if you treated that alarm not as a truth-teller, but as an overprotective part that learned to equate worth with constant doing? What might it say if you asked it directly: "What are you most afraid would happen if I truly rested?"
